'''twistingly''' (twis′ting-li), ''adv.'' In a twisting manner; by twisting or being twisted. ''Bailey'', 1731.

'''twisting-machine''' (twis′ting-ma̤-shēn″), ''n.'' A machine for twisting rope and cördage; a rope-machine.

'''twisting-mill''' (twis′ting-mil), ''n.'' In ''spinning'', a thread-frame.

'''twist-joint''' (twist′joint), ''n.'' A joint formed by laying the ends of two wires past each other a few inches and binding the end of each several times round the other wire: much used in American telegraph-lines.

'''twistle<sup>1</sup>''' (twis′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''twistled'', ppr. ''twistling''. [A freq. of ''twist''.] To twist. ''Jamieson'' (spelled ''twisle, twussle''). [Scotch.]

'''twistle<sup>1</sup>''' (twis′l), ''n.'' [< ''twistle''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] A twist; a wrench. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The L —— ’s cause ne’er got sic a ''twistle''
Sin’ I ha’e min’.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Twa Herds.}}}}

raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|twist|6556|twistle}}</noinclude>described by an object so moving: as, the ''twist'' given to a ball in pitching causes it to curve; the ''twist'' of a billiard-ball in play.

{{smaller block|If he had only allowed for the ''twist''! but he hasn’t, and so the ball goes spinning up straight in the air.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 8.}}
The screw or ''twist'' [in billiards] is made by striking the ball low down, with a sharp, sudden blow.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', III. 676.}}
It is the ''twists'' in the rods that cause the figure to appear in the barrels, and all iron so twisted is called Damascus.
{{right|''W. W. Greener'', The Gun, p. 226.}}}}
'''8.''' Specifically, in firearms—(''a'') The spiral formed by a groove in a rifled piece; the inclination of the grooves of a rifled piece to the axis of the bore.

{{smaller block|Some of the rifles and rifled ordnance in the service are made with grooves which have a very slight ''twist'' at the breech, but the ''twist'' is increased regularly until it reaches the muzzle; this is known as the increasing or gaining ''twist''.
{{right|''Farrow'', Mil. Encyc., I. 727.}}
If the angle of inclination be equal at all points, the ''twist'' is said to be uniform. . . . If the angle increases from the breech to the muzzle, the ''twist'' is called increasing; if the reverse, decreasing.
{{right|''Tidball'', Manual of Artillery, p. 38.}}}}
(''b'') Iron and steel twisted and welded together, used as a material for gun-barrels.—'''9.''' In ''arch.'', the wind of the bed-joint of every course of voussoirs in a skew arch.—'''10.''' In rope, cordage, and the like, the way in which the spiral strands are laid, the number of strands, the degree of turn of the spiral, etc.: as, these two ropes differ in their ''twist''.—'''11.''' A convolution; a curve; a flexure; a bend or turn.

{{smaller block|Unkus, alias Okoco, the Monahegan sachem in the ''twist'' of Pequod River, came to Boston with thirty-seven men.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 319.}}}}
{{smaller block|Knowing every ''twist'' and turn of rock, our drivers brought us at the camping-time almost to the verge of the chaparral.
{{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Erema, lviii.}}}}

'''12.''' A turning about, as on a pivot or axis; a turn; a twirl.
{{smaller block|<poem>A wink of his eye, and a ''twist'' of his head,
Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread.</poem>
{{right|''C. C. Moore'', A Visit from St. Nicholas.}}}}

'''13.''' A wresting out of place; distortion; a wrench; a strain.
{{smaller block|Which ligament keeps the two parts of the joint so firmly in their place that . . . none of the jerks and ''twists'' to which it [the limb] is ordinarily liable . . . can pull them asunder.
{{right|''Paley'', Nat. Theol., viii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Generally, it was after a number of twistings in both ways, from the initial position of no ''twist'', that the transient current settled to its final value.
{{right|''Philos. Mag.'', London, 5th ser., XXIX. 124.}}}}

'''14.''' Figuratively, a peculiar bent, turn, or cast; a variation or perversion from the usual or normal type.
{{smaller block|Heads with some diverting ''twist'' in them — the oddities of authorship please me most.
{{right|''Lamb'', Mackery End.}}}}
{{smaller block|An exclusively scientific training will bring about a mental ''twist'' as surely as an exclusively literary training.
{{right|''Huxley'', Science and Culture.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You might have called him, with his humorous ''twist'',
A kind of human entomologist.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Fitz Adam’s Story.}}}}

'''15.''' An appetite for food. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] — '''16.''' A mixed drink, generally named from the spirit with which it is compounded. [Eng.]
{{smaller block|When he went to the Back Kitchen that night, . . . the gin-''twist'' and devilled turkey had no charms for him.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Pendennis, xxxix.}}}}
'''17.''' In ''dynam.'', a twist-velocity.—'''18.''' In ''math.'': (''a'') A torsional strain or distortion. (''b'') A displacement along and around a screw; a translation combined with a rotation round an axis parallel to the direction of translation; in the non-Euclidean geometry, a compound of two rotations about conjugate polars to the absolute.—{{smaller|'''Damascus twist.''' See ''damascus''.—'''Gaining twist.''' Same as ''increase-twist''.—'''Grape-vine twist.''' See ''grape-vine''.—'''Ramp and twist.''' See ''ramp''.—'''Slack twist,''' a loose twist.—'''Twist drill.''' See ''drill''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Twist of the wrist,''' the movements of pronation and supination, which bring the hand quickly into various positions; hence, quick and adroit use of the hand; dexterity; knack.}}

'''twist''' (twist), ''v.'' [< ME. ''twisten'', ''twysten'' = MD. ''twisten'', twist; cf. MD. D. ''twisten'' = MLG. LG. ''twisten'' = Sw. ''trista'' = Dan. ''triste'', strive, quarrel, = Icel. ''tristra'', divide, scatter: see ''twist'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To unite, as two or more strands or filaments, by winding one about another; hence, to form by twining or rolling into a single thread; spin.
{{smaller block|<poem>The smallest thread
That ever spider ''twisted'' from her womb.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 3. 128.}}}}
{{smaller block|It was worth while to hear the croaking and hollow tones of the old lady, and the pleasant voice of Phœbe, mingling in one ''twisted'' thread of talk.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, v.}}}}

'''2.''' To intertwine; interweave; combine.
{{smaller block|Falsehood is strangely joined and ''twisted'' along with truth.
{{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, ii., Expl.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let earth and hell conspire their worst, their best,
And join their ''twisted'' might.</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, ii. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|His [God’s] great intention was to ''twist'' our duty and our happiness together.
{{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, I. ii.}}}}

'''3.''' To weave; fabricate; compose.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou shalt have her. Was ’t not to this end
That thou began’st to ''twist'' so fine a story?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, i. 1. 313.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Consort both harp and lute, and ''twist'' a song
Pleasant and long.</poem>
{{right|''G. Herbert'', The Church, Easter.}}}}

'''4.''' To wreathe; wind; twine.
{{smaller block|<poem>Green, slender, leaf-clad holly-boughs
Were ''twisted'' gracefu’ round her brows.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', The Vision, i.}}}}

'''5.''' To bend or turn spirally, as by causing both ends to revolve in opposite directions; alter in shape so that parts previously in the same straight line and plane are located in a spiral curve; also, to cause to move spirally or with a progressive rotary motion, as a ball when pitched in a curve, or a billiard-ball when Englished.
{{smaller block|By all that is hirsute and gashly! I cry, taking off my furr’d cap, and ''twisting'' it round my finger, I would not give sixpence for a dozen such.
{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, V. 215.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The fountain . . . playing now
A ''twisted'' snake, and now a rain of pearls.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, Prol.}}}}
{{smaller block|Others [columns] have ''twisted'' fluting. {{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 130.}}
The square rods of prepared iron are first ''twisted'' to give the Damascus figure. {{right|''W. W. Greener'', The Gun, p. 224.}}}}
'''6.''' To curve; bend; deflect: as, to ''twist'' a thing into a serpentine form; ''twisted'' like the letter S.
{{smaller block|<poem>At length a generation more refin’d . . .
Gave them [stools] a ''twisted'' form vermicular.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, i. 30.}}}}
'''7.''' To thrust out of place or shape; contort or distort; pervert; wrench; wrest; warp: used literally or figuratively.
{{smaller block|<poem>There sat . . . the dumb old servitor, on deck,
Winking his eyes, and ''twisted'' all his face.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}
I call it a poor-spirited thing to take up a man’s straightforward words and ''twist'' them.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xi.}}}}
'''8.''' To press hard; wring.
{{smaller block|<poem>She taketh hym by the hand and hard hym ''twiste'',
So secrely that no wight of it wiste.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 761.}}}}
'''9†.''' To lop, as a tree, by cutting off branches or twigs. ''Cath. Ang.''—{{smaller|'''To double and twist.''' See ''double''.—'''To twist round one’s (little) finger,''' to move, mold, or influence (a person) at will; have under complete control or subjection. [Colloq.]—'''To twist the lion’s tail.''' See ''tail''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Twisted bit, Cartesian, cubic.''' See the nouns.—'''Twisted curve.''' See ''skew curve'', under ''curve''.—'''Twisted ironwork,''' iron bars, straps, etc., twisted or plaited together for ornamental purposes: the name of a patented invention introduced about 1870.—'''Twisted leather.''' See ''leather''.—'''Twisted net,''' a machine-made net used for linings in dressmaking, etc., generally of cotton, and composed of three threads.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be intertwined or interwoven. {{smaller block|<poem>Too well he knows the ''twisting'' strings
Of ardent hearts combin’d,
When rent asunder, how they bleed,
How hard to be resign’d.</poem>
{{right|''Young'', Resignation.}}}}
'''2.''' To be wreathed or coiled; wind.
{{smaller block|<poem>O how these arms, these greedy arms, did twine
And strongly ''twist'' about his yielding waist!</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, iv. 12.}}}}
'''3.''' To be bent round and round spirally; also, to move in such a manner or with continuous revolutions.
{{smaller block|The ball comes skimming and ''twisting'' along about three feet from the ground.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|The rod is carefully watched whilst ''twisting'', and, should one part commence to ''twist'' more rapidly than another, a man is ready with a pair of tongs to hold that part of the rod, so that it is prevented from ''twisting''.
{{right|''W. W. Greener'', The Gun, p. 224.}}}}
'''4.''' To curve; circle; revolve; move in a circle or spiral.
{{smaller block|<poem>At noon, or when the lesser wain
Is ''twisting'' round the polar star.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, ci.}}}}
'''5.''' To be bent, turned, or contorted; writhe; squirm.
{{smaller block|The eels lie ''twisting'' in the pangs of death.
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xxi. 413.}}}}
{{smaller block|Its limbs were gnarled, . . . ''twisting'' down almost to the earth. {{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 447.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let him cry like a woman and ''twist'' like an eel.
{{right|''Whittier'', Mogg Megone, i.}}}} '''6†.''' To be parted or cleft in twain; be divided, severed, sundered, or separated.

{{smaller block|The onderstondinge . . . ''tuysteth'' ine tuo, huanne me wylneth of one half to god, and of otherhalf to the wordle.
{{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 159.}}}}

'''twistable''' (twis′tạ-bl), ''a.'' [< ''twist'' + ''-able''.] Capable of being twisted or turned.

{{smaller block|This amendment is ''twistable'' into an advice, an impertinent advice to a foreign nation.
{{right|''New York Tribune'', March 28, 1862.}}}}

'''twisted''' (twis′ted), ''a.'' [< ''twist'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' In ''entom.'', noting a joint of the legs, etc., when the faces tend to turn spirally on the joint, as {{img float|file=century v08 p0360 c3f1.png|width=121px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Twisted Columns.—Cloisters of St. John Lateran, Rome.}}}} if this had been subjected to a twisting force.—'''2.''' In ''bot.'', contorted or bent on itself. In estivation, same as ''convolute''.{{smaller|—'''Twisted column,''' a shaft so shaped as to present the appearance of having been twisted. Columns of this form are frequent in minor orders in Romanesque architecture, and occur in works of the Renaissance.—'''Twisted eglantine.''' See ''honeysuckle'', 1.—'''Twisted pine,''' a stunted pine, ''Pinus contorta'', of the western coast of North America; also, ''P. Teocote'' of Mexico, also called ''candlewood pine''.—'''Twisted suture,''' in ''surg.'', a suture in which the edges of a wound are pierced transversely by a needle over which a thread is wound in figure-of-8 form; a harelip suture.}}

'''twisted-flower''' (twis′ted-flou″ėr), ''n.'' See ''Strophanthus.''

'''twisted-horn''' (twis′ted-hôrn), ''n.'' See ''Helicteres.''

'''twisted-stalk''' (twis′ted-stâk), ''n.'' See ''Streptopus.''

'''twisted-stick''' (twis′ted-stik), ''n.'' See ''Helicteres.''

'''twister''' (twis′tėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''twyster''; < ''twist'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who or that which twists. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') In ''weaving'', the person whose occupation it is to twist or join the threads of one warp to those of another.}}

{{smaller block|Now, in consequence of the “cross” keeping the threads of both the warps in consecutive order, the “''twister''-in” has no difficulty in finding the proper threads to twist together.
{{right|''A. Barlow'', Weaving, p. 311.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') An implement or device used for twisting yarns, threads, cords, etc. (''c'') In ''carp.'', a girder. (''d'') That which is twisted or which moves with a twist, as a ball in cricket or billiards.}}
{{smaller block|The cover-point hitter, that cunning man, goes on to bowl slow ''twisters''.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 8.}}
He has learned the trick of playing with a straight bat the examiner’s most artful ''twisters''.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXXIV. 547.}}}}
{{smaller|(''e'') That which twists, writhes, or contorts.}}
{{smaller block|He . . . ran through the whole electrical pharmacopœia, . . . utilising an induction coil to produce the most powerful but involuntary contortions of the diseased limb. After an extra vigorous ''twister'' the doctor would say, “How does that feel?”
{{right|''Elect. Rev.'' (Eng.), XXIV. 525.}}}}
{{smaller|(''f''†) One who trims trees by lopping. ''Cath. Ang.'' (''g'') A bird that flies with twisting or zigzag flight, as the snipe.}} '''2.''' In the ''manège'', the inner part of the thigh: the proper place to rest upon when on horseback.—'''Labrador twister.''' {{smaller|See the quotation.}}
{{smaller block|Those very small wiry, compactly feathered, weather-tanned birds [woodcock], who appear in October and who are called, perhaps locally, ''Labrador twisters''.
{{right|''H. D. Minot'', Land-Birds and Game-Birds of New England (1877), p. 405.}}}}

'''twisting''' (twis′ting), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''twist'', ''v.''] Torsion.

'''twisting-crook''' (twis′ting-kru̇k), ''n.'' A throw-crook.

'''twisting-forceps''' (twis′ting-fôr″seps), ''n.'' In ''surg.'', same as ''torsion forceps'' (which see, under ''torsion'').

'''twistingly''' (twis′ting-li), ''adv.'' In a twisting manner; by twisting or being twisted. ''Bailey'', 1731.

'''twisting-machine''' (twis′ting-ma̤-shēn″), ''n.'' A machine for twisting rope and cördage; a rope-machine.

'''twisting-mill''' (twis′ting-mil), ''n.'' In ''spinning'', a thread-frame.

'''twist-joint''' (twist′joint), ''n.'' A joint formed by laying the ends of two wires past each other a few inches and binding the end of each several times round the other wire: much used in American telegraph-lines.

'''twistle<sup>1</sup>''' (twis′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''twistled'', ppr. ''twistling''. [A freq. of ''twist''.] To twist. ''Jamieson'' (spelled ''twisle, twussle''). [Scotch.]

'''twistle<sup>1</sup>''' (twis′l), ''n.'' [< ''twistle''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] A twist; a wrench. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The L —— ’s cause ne’er got sic a ''twistle''
Sin’ I ha’e min’.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Twa Herds.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
